questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\sqrt{u},\,u=\operatorname{csc}⁡v,\,v=5x+2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡v\operatorname{cot}⁡v,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=5.
$$

Applying the chain rule twice, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}\cdot \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡v\operatorname{cot}⁡v)\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{csc}⁡(5x+2)}}\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡(5x+2)\operatorname{cot}⁡(5x+2))\cdot 5 \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡(5x+2)\sqrt{\operatorname{csc}⁡(5x+2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we compute ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡(5(0)+2)\sqrt{\operatorname{csc}⁡(5(0)+2)} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡(2)\sqrt{\operatorname{csc}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)={x}^{4}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x-1).$ Then

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=4{x}^{3},\,{v}^{′}(x)=-3\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x-1)\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x-1).
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(4{x}^{3})(\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x-1))+({x}^{4})(-3\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x-1)\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x-1)) \\  & =4{x}^{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x-1)-3{x}^{4}\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x-1)\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x-1) \\  & ={x}^{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x-1)(4-3x\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x-1)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})|}_{x=1} & =(1)^{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(3(1)-1)(4-3(1)\operatorname{cot}⁡(3(1)-1)) \\  & =\operatorname{csc}⁡2(4-3\operatorname{cot}⁡2).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)={sin}^{3}⁡x.$ Then

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2x,\,{v}^{′}(x)=3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(2x)({sin}^{3}⁡x)+({x}^{2})(3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =2x{sin}^{3}⁡x+3{x}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})|}_{x=0} & =2\cdot 0\cdot {sin}^{3}⁡(0)+3\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot {sin}^{2}⁡(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=2x.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2x\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}},\,{v}^{′}(x)=2.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{2x\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}})(2x)-(\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})(2)}{(2x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}-2\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{4{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4{x}^{2}\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Calculating a Derivative Using Multiple Instances of the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as a composite function

$$
y = u^4, \qquad u = \cos{v}, \qquad v = 2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = 4u^3,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d v} = -\sin{v},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm d x} = 2.
$$

Applying now the chain rule twice, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}\cdot \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} \\  & =4{u}^{3}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot (2) \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{3}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\cdot (2) \\  & =-8{cos}^{3}⁡2x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x) = e^{-2x}$ and $v(x)=\tan{(x^2)}.$ Then

$$
u'(x) = -2e^{-2x}, \qquad v'(x) = 2x\sec^2(x^2).
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate both $u$ and $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(-2{e}^{-2x})\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})+{e}^{-2x}\cdot 2x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2}) \\  & =2{e}^{-2x}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})+x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})) \\  & =2{e}^{-2x}(x{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})-\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=e^{3x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=2^x +1.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x) = 3e^{3x}, \qquad v'(x) = 2^x \ln 2.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}	&= \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \[5pt]
			        			&=\dfrac{3e^{3x} \cdot  \left( 2^{x}+1\right) - e^{3x} \cdot \left(2^x \cdot \ln2\right)}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\[5pt]
							&=\dfrac{3e^{3x}2^{x} + 3e^{3x} - e^{3x}2^{x}\ln 2}{\left(2^{ x}+1 \right)^2}\[5pt]
							&=\dfrac{e^{3x}  \left( 3(2^{x}) - 2^{x} \ln 2 +3\right)}{\left(2^{x}+1 \right)^2}
		}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Sometimes, we need to combine multiple rules of differentiation to differentiate a given function. As a reminder, the product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule are stated below.

- Product rule: $\hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ u(x) \cdot v(x) \right] = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x)$

- Quotient rule: $\hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ \dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)} \right] = \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2}$

- Chain rule: $\hspace{.5cm} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d}x } \left[ u(v(x)) \right] = u'(v(x))\cdot v'(x)$
